symptoms: P0 alert: 95% of payment requests timing out, latency_p99=28s, error_rate=95%
error_log:
ERROR [payments-api] HikariPool-1: Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms
ERROR [payments-api] PSQLException: FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections
ERROR [payments-api] Connection pool exhausted: active=100/100, idle=0, waiting=342
WARN  [payments-api] Slow query detected: SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id=? took 27823ms
root_cause: Database connection pool exhausted due to a slow query (missing index on transactions.account_id) causing connections to be held longer than usual, eventually exhausting the pool.
fix_applied: Added index on transactions.account_id, increased connection pool max from 100 to 200, killed long-running queries.

symptoms: 100% of JWT validation calls failing with 401 Unauthorized, redis cache completely unreachable
error_log:
ERROR [auth-service] redis.exceptions.ConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to redis-cache:6379. Connection refused.
ERROR [auth-service] JWT validation cache miss — fallback to DB
ERROR [auth-service] DB connection refused: too many connections (max_conn=500, current=501)
FATAL [auth-service] Cannot validate tokens: cache AND database unreachable
root_cause: Redis cache OOM-killed by the host OS (memory limit exceeded), causing the auth-service to fall back entirely to the database which immediately hit its connection limit under the surge of queries.
fix_applied: Restarted Redis with higher memory limit (4GB → 8GB), flushed DB connection pool, rolled out auth-service pods to reset stuck connections.

symptoms: Checkout service 503 errors, DB replica lag at 1800 seconds, writes queuing up
error_log:
ERROR [checkout-db] replication slot 'checkout_replica_1' inactive for 1823 seconds
ERROR [checkout-db] WAL log size: 48GB (threshold: 10GB)
ERROR [checkout-service] Read replica connection timed out after 30s
WARN  [checkout-db] pg_replication_slots: inactive slot consuming WAL, disk 87% full
root_cause: Inactive replication slot caused WAL accumulation, filling disk to 87% and starving the DB of write capacity. The slot was inactive because a replica was silently disconnected after a network partition.
fix_applied: Dropped inactive replication slot, cleaned WAL files, reconnected replica, added monitoring alert for WAL size.
story: On-call engineer first attempted an immediate service restart of the checkout-db primary, hoping it would clear the replica lag. After restarting, the WAL accumulation resumed within 60 seconds — the inactive replication slot was still present and still consuming WAL. Disk hit 91% within 3 minutes of the restart, writes stalled again, and the 503 errors returned at the same rate. The restart bought zero time. Root cause investigation then revealed the true fix: the inactive slot had to be explicitly dropped before WAL would stop growing.

symptoms: Kafka consumer lag 500k+, zero throughput, OOM errors in consumers
error_log:
ERROR [order-queue] java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
ERROR [order-queue] KafkaConsumer: poll() took 34521ms, exceeding max.poll.interval.ms=30000
ERROR [order-queue] Consumer group order-processor: rebalancing triggered
WARN  [order-queue] GC overhead limit exceeded: 98% of time spent in GC
ERROR [order-queue] Offset commit failed: consumer group rebalancing
root_cause: A large batch of oversized messages (avg 2MB vs normal 10KB) caused the JVM heap to fill during deserialization. This triggered GC storms, which exceeded max.poll.interval.ms, causing repeated consumer group rebalances and zero net throughput.
fix_applied: Increased consumer JVM heap from 2GB to 6GB, reduced max.poll.records from 500 to 50 for large message topics, deployed fix to cap message size at 100KB at producer level.

symptoms: Search returning stale results, indexer pod crashlooping, Elasticsearch cluster yellow
error_log:
ERROR [search-indexer] elasticsearch.exceptions.ConnectionTimeout: Connection timed out after 30s
ERROR [search-indexer] BulkIndexError: 342 document(s) failed to index
ERROR [search-indexer] Elasticsearch cluster health: YELLOW — 3 unassigned shards
ERROR [search-indexer] Circuit breaker open: [parent] Data too large, data for [<http_request>] would be [2.1gb/2.0gb]
root_cause: Elasticsearch JVM heap circuit breaker tripped after a large product catalog import (2M records) exhausted heap. Unassigned shards appeared because a data node ran out of disk space and was evicted from the cluster.
fix_applied: Freed disk space on ES data node, re-enabled the evicted node, forced shard reallocation, throttled the catalog import to 10k records/batch.

symptoms: Intermittent 500 errors on payment processing, SSL handshake failures to payment gateway
error_log:
ERROR [payments-api] SSLError: certificate verify failed: certificate has expired
ERROR [payments-api] requests.exceptions.SSLError: HTTPSConnectionPool: Max retries exceeded
ERROR [payments-api] Payment gateway connection refused after 3 retries
WARN  [payments-api] TLS certificate for api.stripe.com expires in: -2 days
root_cause: TLS certificate for the payment gateway integration expired 2 days prior. Certificate rotation automation had silently failed 30 days earlier due to a permissions change on the secrets manager role.
fix_applied: Manually renewed TLS certificate via Let's Encrypt, rotated secret in AWS Secrets Manager, fixed IAM role permissions for cert-manager, added 30-day expiry alert.

symptoms: Login latency spike to 12s, auth service pods OOMKilled, session creation failing
error_log:
ERROR [auth-service] OOMKilled: container auth-service exceeded memory limit 512Mi
ERROR [auth-service] bcrypt hash computation took 9823ms (expected <100ms)
ERROR [auth-service] Session store write timeout: redis connection pool exhausted (pool_size=20, waiting=87)
WARN  [auth-service] bcrypt cost factor: 14 (recommended: 10-12 for production latency)
root_cause: bcrypt cost factor was accidentally set to 14 (max is typically 12) during a security hardening PR. Each login attempt consumed 9+ seconds of CPU and ~200MB of memory, causing OOM kills.
fix_applied: Rolled back bcrypt cost factor to 12, increased pod memory limit to 2Gi, scaled auth-service deployment to 8 replicas.

symptoms: All checkout writes failing, DB primary unresponsive, auto-failover not triggering
error_log:
ERROR [checkout-db] FATAL: the database system is in recovery mode
ERROR [checkout-db] PgBouncer: server login failed: FATAL: the database system is in recovery mode
ERROR [checkout-service] PG connection pool: all connections returning error
WARN  [patroni] Leader lease lost! Last leader: checkout-db-0, new election in progress
WARN  [patroni] Failover inhibited: minimum replication lag not met (lag=180s, threshold=10s)
root_cause: Primary DB ran out of disk (WAL accumulation from a forgotten long-running transaction held open for 3 hours). Patroni's automatic failover was inhibited because the replica lag exceeded the configured threshold (10s), creating a split-brain avoidance deadlock.
fix_applied: Terminated the long-running transaction, freed disk by truncating old WAL, manually triggered Patroni failover after confirming replica was caught up.
story: The on-call engineer's first instinct was to trigger an immediate restart of the checkout-db-0 primary pod, expecting Patroni to elect the replica as the new leader during the restart. The restart fired — but Patroni refused to promote the replica because the replication lag was 180 seconds, exceeding its safety threshold of 10s. The primary came back up in recovery mode with the same disk-full condition, and all writes continued to fail. The restart wasted 12 minutes and left the system in an identical broken state. The actual fix required first killing the long-running transaction to stop WAL growth, then manually freeing disk, and finally issuing a forced Patroni switchover after verifying the replica had caught up.

symptoms: Order processing stopped, Kafka broker showing under-replicated partitions, broker disk 100%
error_log:
ERROR [kafka-broker-2] LEADER_NOT_AVAILABLE: leader for topic orders-v2 partition 4 is not available
ERROR [kafka-broker-2] DiskFull: Cannot write to log segment — disk usage: 100%
ERROR [order-queue] org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerFencedException: older transactional producer attempt to resume
WARN  [kafka-broker-2] UnderReplicatedPartitions: 12 partitions have ISR size < min.insync.replicas
root_cause: Kafka broker disk filled to 100% because log.retention.hours was changed to 168 (7 days) from 24h without increasing disk capacity. This caused log segment writes to fail, leading to under-replicated partitions and producer fence errors.
fix_applied: Added 500GB EBS volume to broker-2, rebalanced partition leaders, reverted retention to 24h, set up disk utilization alert at 70%.

symptoms: Payments degraded: 60% timeout rate, high database query latency, no obvious connection errors
error_log:
WARN  [payments-api] Slow query: SELECT p.*, a.balance FROM payments p JOIN accounts a ON p.account_id=a.id WHERE p.status='pending' took 24891ms
ERROR [payments-api] HikariPool: getConnection() timed out after 30000ms
WARN  [payments-api] Active threads waiting for DB connection: 187
ERROR [payments-api] Transaction rollback: lock wait timeout exceeded
INFO  [payments-api] Connection pool: active=100, idle=0, waiting=187
root_cause: Connection pool exhaustion caused by a slow JOIN query lacking an index on payments.status. Root cause is the same as INC-001 (missing index + pool exhaustion) but manifesting as high latency instead of direct connection errors — the query plan changed after a table statistics update.
fix_applied: Added composite index on (payments.status, payments.account_id), ANALYZE on payments table, increased pool size temporarily.

symptoms: Spike in 401 errors, users being logged out, session tokens invalid — Redis shows no errors
error_log:
ERROR [auth-service] JWT verification failed: SignatureVerificationError: invalid signature
ERROR [auth-service] Token decode failed: ExpiredSignatureError: Signature has expired
WARN  [auth-service] JWT secret key hash mismatch — new secret detected
ERROR [auth-service] Session cache: Key not found for token prefix v2_
INFO  [auth-service] Config hot-reload triggered: jwt_secret_key changed
root_cause: JWT secret key was rotated via config hot-reload during peak hours. All existing tokens signed with the old key immediately became invalid. Root cause pattern matches INC-002 (auth service mass-failure) but the mechanism is different: key rotation instead of Redis failure.
fix_applied: Rolled back JWT secret to previous version, planned gradual rotation with dual-key support (accept old + new key during transition).

symptoms: Checkout service extremely slow writes (8s+), no disk errors, replication appears healthy
error_log:
WARN  [checkout-db] autovacuum: found 42819342 dead tuples on table orders — vacuum threshold exceeded by 41819342
WARN  [checkout-db] Table bloat ratio: orders=89%, order_items=76%
ERROR [checkout-service] UPDATE orders SET status=? WHERE id=? took 8241ms
ERROR [checkout-service] Lock contention detected: waiting on relation orders (size: 847GB)
INFO  [checkout-db] seq_scan on orders: 4821 scans/hour (table: 847GB, index usage: 12%)
root_cause: Autovacuum was disabled on the orders table to avoid I/O contention (a previous bad change). 43M dead tuples accumulated causing severe table bloat (89%) and sequential scans on an 847GB table, slowing all writes. Same infrastructure class as INC-008 (checkout-db degraded) but different root cause: vacuum instead of disk/WAL.
fix_applied: Re-enabled autovacuum with aggressive settings, ran manual VACUUM ANALYZE, rebuilt table with pg_repack to reclaim space without locking.
story: Seeing 8-second write latency on checkout-db with no obvious disk or replication issues, the on-call engineer restarted the checkout-db service (both the application tier and the database connection pooler, PgBouncer) as an immediate mitigation step. For exactly 90 seconds after restart, write latency appeared to drop to 2s — but this was simply the brief window while the connection pool was empty and before the table bloat reasserted itself. Within 2 minutes the write latency climbed back to 8s as new queries resumed sequential scans on the 847GB orders table. The restart had no effect on the 43M dead tuples or the seq_scan rate; the table bloat was the root cause and only VACUUM ANALYZE addressed it.

symptoms: Order consumer throughput dropped 80%, lag growing, no OOM errors this time
error_log:
WARN  [order-queue] Consumer poll latency: 18s (max.poll.interval.ms=30s)
ERROR [order-queue] CorruptRecordException: Record is corrupt at offset 8841923 in partition orders-v2-7
ERROR [order-queue] DeserializationException: Failed to deserialize value from topic orders-v2
WARN  [order-queue] Skipping poison pill message at offset 8841923 — DLQ write failed
ERROR [order-queue] Dead letter queue orders-dlq: topic does not exist
root_cause: 12 poison pill messages (corrupt serialization from a producer bug) caused consumer threads to stall trying to write to a DLQ topic that had been accidentally deleted. Similar failure class to INC-004 (order-queue stall) but mechanism is message corruption, not heap exhaustion.
fix_applied: Re-created DLQ topic, deployed consumer with skip-on-corrupt logic, patched producer serialization bug.

symptoms: Search index 6 hours out of date, indexer running but no documents indexed since midnight
error_log:
ERROR [search-indexer] ElasticsearchException: index [products_v3] blocked: FORBIDDEN/8/index write blocked
ERROR [search-indexer] ClusterBlockException: index [products_v3] is read-only (read_only_allow_delete=true)
WARN  [elasticsearch] Low disk watermark [85%] exceeded on node es-data-1
INFO  [search-indexer] 842 indexing requests rejected by Elasticsearch in last hour
root_cause: Elasticsearch automatically set the products_v3 index to read-only when the data node disk exceeded the 85% low watermark (reached 92%). Same infrastructure class as INC-005 (search-indexer failure) but triggered by gradual disk growth over weeks rather than a sudden import.
fix_applied: Deleted old index snapshots, added EBS volume to es-data-1, cleared read-only block via cluster settings API, set up 80% disk alert.

symptoms: Payment service P1: 35% of charges failing with 'service unavailable', connection errors to DB spike
error_log:
ERROR [payments-api] HikariPool: Connection pool usage at 97% — active=97/100, idle=3
ERROR [payments-api] PSQLException: ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update
ERROR [payments-api] deadlock detected: Process 47281 waits for ShareLock on transaction 3891742
WARN  [payments-api] Long-running transaction detected: txn_id=3891742 age=842s
ERROR [payments-api] Connection pool exhausted after 30s wait
root_cause: A long-running payment transaction (14 minutes) held row-level locks, causing deadlocks and serialization failures for concurrent payment attempts. Pool exhaustion followed as connections piled up waiting for locks. Same pool exhaustion pattern as INC-001 and INC-010, but caused by lock contention not missing indexes.
fix_applied: Killed the stuck transaction (pg_terminate_backend), set statement_timeout=60s and lock_timeout=10s, added idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=120s.
story: When the deadlock storm and 35% failure rate appeared, the on-call engineer rolled a full service restart of the payments-api pods — a common first step for connection pool exhaustion. The pods restarted and briefly the pool appeared healthy: active connections dropped to 0. But within 45 seconds the failure rate climbed back to 35%. The restart flushed the application-side connection pool, but the offending long-running transaction (txn_id=3891742, age=842s) was still open on the database side, still holding its ShareLock. New connections immediately stacked up waiting for the same lock. The correct fix required using pg_terminate_backend() to kill the stuck database transaction directly, which no amount of application-layer restarts could accomplish.
